data.title: Trump's Iran strike threat returns, but why aren't oil prices surging?
data.description:
Oil prices struggled to rally on Thursday despite reports that US President Donald Trump was considering fresh strikes against Iran, as rising inventories and recovering Middle Eastern exports kept traders focused on the prospect of excess supply.

Brent crude futures edged up 0.18% to $92.12 a barrel at 02:37 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate slipped 0.11% to $83.17.

The restrained response followed Wednesday's 1.3% fall in Brent. With a possible new military campaign under discussion, the central question is why escalating threats are no longer enough to lift crude prices decisively.

Brent crude oil price: Trump considers further strikes

Axios reported on Thursday that Trump was weighing a joint operation with Israel against Iran, although no decision had been announced.

The White House has sought assessments of possible Iranian retaliation, including attacks on oil and gas facilities in Gulf states.

Gulf leaders are urging restraint, while Israeli officials have raised concerns about suspected Iranian weapons development. Those allegations remain disputed, and Trump indicated on Wednesday that another offensive was not imminent.

Security risks are already tangible, as recent tanker incidents and attacks on regional infrastructure have complicated shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil supplies.

Yet traders appear reluctant to price a prolonged interruption before one materialises and changes the flow of exports.

Vandana Hari, founder of Vanda Insights, described crude as caught between a “persistent geopolitical risk premium” and increasingly bearish expectations of a sizeable surplus, in comments to Reuters on Wednesday.

Oil price forecast: Recovering supply and US stockpiles restrain prices

The International Energy Agency reported that global oil production climbed by 2.3 million barrels a day in October to 105.4 million, as Gulf exports recovered despite continued attacks.

Observed worldwide inventories rose by 52 million barrels, their first monthly increase since June. The agency expects supply to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, although diesel supplies and onshore stocks remain tight.

US data reinforced the bearish case. Commercial crude inventories increased by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million in the week ended 13 November, according to figures released Wednesday by the Energy Information Administration.

Gasoline stocks rose 5.2 million barrels, while distillate inventories gained 1.6 million. Those builds suggest refiners and distributors have more immediate supply available, weakening the case for a sustained crude rally.

But the recovery remains exposed to sudden setbacks.

Recent attacks near Hormuz “highlight the fragility of this recovery”, Sparta Commodities analyst Abhishek Kumar said in comments reported by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.

His warning underscores that an improving global crude balance does not mean tankers, refineries or fuel markets are secure.

Could another escalation push Brent back towards $100?

An actual interruption to Gulf shipments could change the calculation quickly, particularly if retaliation damages export terminals or closes shipping routes.

Goldman Sachs recently raised its December Brent forecast to $105 from $90, reflecting the risk of renewed supply losses. That estimate is a forecast rather than a guaranteed response to Trump's deliberations.

However, without significant disruption, recovering OPEC+ output and stronger Russian crude exports could continue limiting gains.

ING strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson wrote on Wednesday that they expect the oil balance to loosen as supply recovers, “limiting the scope for a sustained rebound in prices”.

Higher US interest-rate expectations and a firm dollar may also restrain consumption and make oil more expensive for overseas buyers.

The next decisive signals will come from Washington's military choices, tanker traffic through Hormuz and subsequent inventory figures.

data.title: Anthropic IPO prices at $83 a share as ANT prepares Thursday debut
data.description:
Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, according to CNBC and Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, $5 above the top of the $70–$78 range in the company's latest SEC filing.

Class A shares in the Claude developer are due to begin trading on Thursday, 19 November, on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT.

The $83 price has not yet been locked in a prospectus supplement.

As of late evening in London on 18 November, no Form 424B4 had appeared on EDGAR, and Anthropic had not published a pricing announcement on its newsroom or IPO site.

Until a filing appears, these figures should be read as reported terms, not as a confirmed prospectus price.

Bloomberg also said the size of the offering has increased, without disclosing a new share count.

The marketed deal, in Amendment No. 3 to Anthropic's Form S-1, filed on 17 November, was 825 million Class A shares — 801,351,354 sold by the company and 23,648,646 by existing holders.

On that marketed count, $83 a share would raise $68.475 billion before underwriting discounts, an Invezz calculation.

Actual gross proceeds would be higher if the deal was upsized, as Bloomberg reported. Anthropic would not receive the proceeds from the secondary shares. A separate $26 billion private placement of non-voting Class N shares is due to close at the IPO price.

How does $83 compare with the filed range?

The official range was never raised in a filing. Amendment No. 3 still estimated $70.00 to $78.00 a share. At $78, the 825 million shares would have raised $64.35 billion gross, as set out in our note on Anthropic's $70–$78 IPO price range.

Earlier on Wednesday, CNBC reported that Anthropic was considering selling more than 825 million shares and was weighing a price well above $80.

The Wall Street Journal had reported on 17 November that Anthropic expected to price above $80, and said that would value the company at about $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion.

The prospectus granted the underwriters, represented by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, a 30-day option to buy up to 123.75 million additional Class A shares. Whether that greenshoe was resized with any upsizing of the base deal has not been disclosed.

What valuation does $83 imply?

The filing does not state a single official valuation, and the final figure will depend on the share count used, including any upsizing.

Coverage of the prospectus has put the fully diluted value at about $1.405 trillion at the $78 top of the range. A like-for-like move to $83 would imply about $1.50 trillion. That is an illustration, not a number in a pricing prospectus, and it would change if more shares have been added.

How strong was demand?

CNBC reported on Wednesday morning that institutional demand was around $400 billion and that retail demand was approaching $100 billion. Those figures were described as indications of interest, not binding orders.

What happens next?

Trading is scheduled to start on Thursday under the ANT ticker. Nasdaq, in Data Technical News #2026-28, said Anthropic's Class A common stock is expected to begin trading on 19 November.

Hargreaves Lansdown has told UK applicants that trading is expected from 2:30pm London time (9:30am ET). Investors who received an allocation pay the IPO price; anyone buying once the shares are listed pays the market price. A Form 424B4, when it appears, would be the official confirmation of the price, the final share count and any change to the greenshoe.

If ANT starts trading on 19 November, MSCI has said it would decide on early inclusion no later than before the open of the third trading day, which would be Monday, 23 November. If the stock qualifies, addition would be effective as of the close on 30 November, or 1 December.

FTSE Russell has deferred fast entry because of Thanksgiving: Russell US addition, if confirmed, would be effective 14 December, and FTSE GEIS on 21 December. Nasdaq has not issued a notice adding ANT to the Nasdaq-100. The S&P 500 is not in prospect at listing.

📅 We are tracking the price, valuation and timetable on our Anthropic IPO date, valuation and ticker hub.

Thursday's first trade will test whether that demand holds up in public.

data.title: Why is Nvidia stock falling over 2% on Wednesday?
data.description:
Nvidia shares NVDA fell 2.2% on Wednesday, extending their decline to a fifth consecutive session, as the US House Committee on Energy and Commerce demanded a formal briefing from the chipmaker over alleged export control violations and former CEO Jensen Huang's reported links to a suspected Chinese spy.

Representative Brett Guthrie, chairman of the committee, sent a letter to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress requesting that company officials appear before lawmakers no later than December 2.

The inquiry focuses on whether Nvidia circumvented federal restrictions intended to prevent advanced artificial intelligence technology from reaching China.

Lawmakers are also examining allegations that a senior company official attempted to interfere with a federal investigation.

The developments add to the pressure on Nvidia as it navigates a leadership transition and scrutiny over national security concerns, despite strong quarterly results and an upbeat revenue outlook.

Congressional probe focuses on export control allegations

In his letter, Guthrie said the reported events raised questions about Nvidia's compliance with federal export laws and the effectiveness of its security controls.

The congressional investigation centres on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of helping Chinese companies circumvent US export restrictions.

On November 16, the Justice Department and Commerce Department publicly confirmed a joint criminal investigation into the company.

Reports have also linked Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is alleged to have a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, to suspected Chinese intelligence activities.

According to Guthrie's letter, investigators are examining claims that she established a network of companies across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia hardware.

Lawmakers are also looking into allegations that the Commerce Department transferred its initial investigation into Megaspeed to the Justice Department last year after Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce officials seeking information about the inquiry.

These allegations have not been established as findings of wrongdoing by Nvidia.

Leadership transition adds to investor concerns

The controversy has coincided with significant changes at Nvidia's senior leadership level.

On November 8, Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in an internal email to employees and said the company's board had launched an independent investigation into national security concerns raised by media reports.

Four days later, he announced his departure from company leadership.

Kress, Nvidia's former chief financial officer, took over as interim CEO while the company works with an external firm to find a permanent replacement.

The uncertainty has weighed on investor sentiment, with Nvidia shares declining for five consecutive trading sessions and facing the prospect of a seventh consecutive weekly loss.

However, Wall Street analysts have pointed to the company's latest financial results as evidence that demand for AI infrastructure remains strong.

Nvidia reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $2.68 per share, beating analyst expectations by 21 cents.

Revenue reached $115.84 billion, up 103.2% from a year earlier and $7.13 billion above forecasts.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, compared with analyst estimates of $124.89 billion.

The forecast assumes no data centre computing revenue from China.

Analysts remain positive on Nvidia's outlook

Several Wall Street firms have maintained positive views on Nvidia despite the leadership uncertainty.

RBC reiterated its Outperform rating, citing demand that continues to exceed supply, a product roadmap extending over the next three years and limited near-term competitive risks due to industry supply constraints.

The firm also highlighted rising supply purchase commitments as evidence of strong demand visibility.

Morgan Stanley maintained its Overweight rating, pointing to strong demand for AI computing and Nvidia's competitive position.

Its analysts also viewed the company's willingness to provide forward-looking commentary as a positive.

Wedbush raised its price target to $293 from $275 while retaining an Outperform rating.

The firm said Nvidia's near- and medium-term demand outlook remained unchanged despite Huang's departure.

The company also has $227.3 billion remaining under its share buyback authorisation.

Kress described returning capital to shareholders as a top priority during the earnings call and said Nvidia could fully utilise the remaining authorisation by fiscal 2028.

Jefferies said the buyback programme offered another potential source of support for the stock, while noting that investors still need greater visibility into the company's strategic direction following the leadership transition.

Meanwhile, Kress said Nvidia was raising its fiscal 2028 outlook and expected revenue growth of approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% previously and on a higher fiscal 2027 base.

data.title: Nvidia earnings: investors still need answers to two key questions
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) more than doubled its quarterly revenue to nearly $116 billion in its fiscal Q3 and issued impressive guidance for the future as well.

But buying NVDA shares this morning means betting on growth that still has to be earned. Two questions matter for that bet:

  1. Can Nvidia keep delivering new chips on schedule and winning big orders without Jensen Huang?
  2. If tighter US rules choke off Chinese demand served through Singapore, can it turn those same chips into just as much profit somewhere else?

Nvidia stock is currently down nearly 35% versus its year-to-date high.

Key man risk remains alive for Nvidia stock

While the media narrative this morning is how Nvidia earnings essentially silence the “key man” risk, it’s worth noting that the company’s quarter ended Oct. 25 – about two weeks before its board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation.

Simply put, Huang ran Nvidia for the entire quarter.

So, the earnings beat, and even the guidance, tells investors that orders Nvidia had already secured translated into strong sales. The real test for interim CEO Colette Kress and NVDA stock actually begins with the “next round of orders.”

Kress told CNBC that key cloud customers were still asking for more computing power.

The harder question is whether those customers will keep committing billions to Nvidia’s next generation of chips.

A delayed launch or a large order that goes elsewhere could dent future earnings, turning investors less willing to pay a premium for each dollar Nvidia earns.

China remains a key overhang on NVDA shares

A chip can sit in a Singapore data centre and still do work for a customer in China – the new US rules target some of that remote access.

Nvidia recorded $11.05 billion, about 9.5% of quarterly sales, from direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong.

Its print leaves the amount of Chinese demand served through Singapore unknown.

On CNBC, Jim Cramer asked whether other buyers could absorb chips Nvidia might stop shipping to the region without pushing prices down.

Kress explained how Nvidia checks who will use the chips and whether data centres are ready.

But she gave no indication of how quickly alternative buyers could take delivery or whether they would pay the same price.

That remains a key overhang on Nvidia shares.

Technical setup warrants caution on Nvidia

Even from a technical perspective, NVDA shares have not turned attractive yet.

The AI darling currently sits firmly below major moving averages (MAs), with an RSI in the early 20s indicating intense selling pressure.

That said, Wall Street hasn’t thrown in the towel on Nvidia yet.

The consensus rating on the chip-maker remains at Strong Buy, with the mean price target of about $258 indicating massive upside potential from current levels.

data.title: When could Anthropic stock join the MSCI, Russell, FTSE and Nasdaq-100?
data.description:
Index funds may be among the larger buyers of Anthropic stock after it lists, but they will not all arrive on the first day, and they will not all arrive at once.

Anthropic is due to price its IPO on 18 November and to start trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on 19 November under the ticker ANT, as set out in Nasdaq Data Technical News #2026-28 and the company's latest S-1 amendment. The official range is still $70–$78 a share for 825 million Class A shares.

The timetable is now clearer than it was at the start of the roadshow, and slower than some early commentary suggested. Thanksgiving has pushed two FTSE Russell additions later into December. The S&P 500 is not in prospect at listing at all.

When could Anthropic join MSCI?

MSCI has published the rule, not the decision. In a 12 November announcement for its Global Standard indexes, it said it would apply its usual methodology for large IPOs.

To qualify for early inclusion, the stock must meet MSCI's eligibility rules, with the exception of the usual length-of-trading and liquidity screens, and must have a company full market capitalisation of at least 1.8 times the Interim Market Size-Segment Cutoff, plus a free-float-adjusted market capitalisation of at least 1.8 times one-half of that cutoff, measured at the close of the first or second trading day.

Any greenshoe publicly announced as exercised before MSCI's decision would be included in those calculations.

The decision would be announced no earlier than the first day of trading and no later than before the opening of the third trading day. If the first trade is on 19 November, that third session would be Monday, 23 November. Early inclusions are usually effective as of the close of the tenth trading day, but if that date falls close to a scheduled review, the addition is aligned with the review instead.

On that basis, if ANT begins trading on 19 November and meets the tests, inclusion would be effective as of the close on 30 November 2026, or 1 December, coinciding with the November 2026 Index Review. That remains a conditional outcome.

Why did FTSE Russell push the dates back?

Because a standard fast-entry calendar would have landed next to Thanksgiving.

In two informative notices dated 13 November, FTSE Russell said it will confirm after the first day of trading whether Anthropic meets the tests, and will issue a further notice after that session if it does.

For the Russell US Equity Indexes, the fast-entry threshold is $17.942 billion of investable market capitalisation. The usual rule would add an eligible IPO after the close of the fifth trading day. If the first trade is on 19 or 20 November, FTSE Russell said the stock would instead be added with the December semi-annual reconstitution, after the close on Friday, 11 December, effective at the open on Monday, 14 December, if it meets the criteria.

For the FTSE Global Equity Index Series, the current fast-entry thresholds for FTSE North America are $43.741 billion of full market capitalisation and $14.580 billion of investable market capitalisation. If ANT qualifies, it would be added with the December review, after the close on Friday, 18 December, effective at the open on Monday, 21 December. Until those notices appear, inclusion is not confirmed.

Could ANT enter the Nasdaq-100 in December?

It might be considered. It has not been added. Nasdaq has not published a notice naming ANT as a Nasdaq-100 constituent.

Under the Nasdaq-100 methodology, a newly listed security can be considered for fast-track inclusion if it meets the index's eligibility and ranking tests.

The next scheduled reconstitution is widely expected to take effect on 21 December 2026, and some secondary reports have already treated that date as a likely entry point for Anthropic. That is a reading of the rulebook, not an official Nasdaq announcement, and should not be confused with the MSCI and FTSE Russell calendars above.

Why is the S&P 500 not in play at listing?

Because it still requires a seasoning period and a profitability test, and S&P Dow Jones Indices has declined to waive either for megacap companies.

In the results of a June 2026 consultation, S&P DJI left the S&P 500 rules unchanged: IPOs should have traded on an eligible exchange for at least 12 months, and companies must have positive GAAP net income from continuing operations in the most recent quarter and in the sum of the most recent four consecutive quarters.

If ANT lists on 19 November 2026, the 12-month clock would run into mid-November 2027. The profitability test is a separate hurdle.

Anthropic's prospectus shows a history of GAAP net losses, including a net loss of $104.0 billion for the nine months ended 30 September 2026, of which $94.3 billion was fair-value changes on convertible notes and related instruments.

Even if much of that loss is non-cash, it is still a GAAP net loss, so the stock would not meet the earnings screen at listing.

The broader S&P Total Market Index has a separate fast-track process for eligible IPOs, which Reuters noted on 12 November. That is not an S&P 500 inclusion.

How much passive demand is expected?

The useful estimate on the table is already a few days old, and the calendar has since moved.

Index-rebalance firm Intropic estimated that passive demand from index-tracking funds would account for about 28% of the shares on offer, or roughly $19 billion.

FTSE Russell's Thanksgiving deferral means part of that buying, if it materialises, now sits in mid-December for the Russell US indexes and in the third week of December for FTSE GEIS. MSCI's potential 1 December effective date is still relatively early.

The $19 billion figure should be read as an estimate prepared against a faster calendar, not as a confirmed order for the first two weeks of trading.

Index funds that do buy will be doing so because the rules require it, which can still matter in early trading, but it does not guarantee a higher price.

Investors who want exposure through an index fund will need to check whether the tracker they hold follows a benchmark that is actually adding the stock, and on which date.

Buying ANT directly once trading begins is a different route.

📘 Our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock covers opening an account for US-listed shares once trading begins.

📅 The listing timetable, the official range and the valuation are collected on our Anthropic IPO date, valuation and ticker hub.

data.title: Evening digest: Anthropic IPO demand surges as gold and oil prices fall
data.description:
US markets faced mixed signals on Wednesday as Anthropic prepared to price its highly anticipated initial public offering amid exceptional investor demand.

Oil prices fell more than 2% after US crude and fuel inventories recorded larger-than-expected increases, while gold dropped to its lowest level in more than a year as hawkish Federal Reserve commentary strengthened the dollar and Treasury yields.

Nvidia shares also extended their losing streak as US lawmakers sought answers over alleged export control violations and reports involving former CEO Jensen Huang.

Anthropic IPO attracts nearly $500B in demand

Anthropic is considering increasing the size of its IPO and pricing shares above the initial range of $70 to $78, CNBC reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The company closed its order books on Tuesday, with institutional demand reaching approximately $400 billion and retail demand approaching $100 billion.

These indications of interest are non-binding, and the final offering terms remain subject to change.

Anthropic initially planned to offer 825 million shares, potentially raising up to $64.35 billion at the top of its proposed price range.

The company is expected to announce its final IPO price after Wednesday's market close.

The listing is a significant test of investor appetite for AI companies.

Anthropic's proposed offering has attracted more demand than SpaceX's IPO, which raised $85.7 billion in June.

The company's prospectus reported revenue of $33.24 billion for the nine months ended September 30, an increase of approximately 1,200% year over year.

However, it recorded a net loss of $104 billion during the period, largely reflecting changes in the fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities.

Its run-rate revenue reached approximately $81 billion at the end of October.

Oil prices fall as US inventories surge

Oil prices declined after the US Energy Information Administration reported larger-than-expected increases in crude and fuel inventories.

Brent crude futures fell 1.7% to $91.50 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate dropped 3.7% to $82.80.

Both benchmarks were on track to lose approximately 20% in November amid expectations of a global supply surplus.

US crude inventories increased by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week ended November 13, significantly exceeding expectations for a 58,000-barrel rise.

Gasoline stocks climbed by 5.2 million barrels, compared with forecasts for a 1.6 million-barrel increase.

Distillate inventories also rose by 1.6 million barrels.

Rising Middle Eastern exports have added to expectations of greater supply, although the US-Iran conflict continues to threaten shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Recent attacks on commercial vessels and infrastructure in the region have highlighted the risks to oil transportation.

Gold hits one-year low as rate hike expectations rise

Gold prices dropped 3% to $3,729.28 an ounce, reaching their lowest level since September 2025. US gold futures declined 3.4% to $3,732.10.

A stronger US dollar and rising Treasury yields weighed on the precious metal as investors increased expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank needed a more aggressive response to inflation, either through a 50-basis-point increase in December or a faster pace of rate hikes in 2027. Other officials have also indicated that additional increases may be necessary.

Markets priced in a 92% probability of a 25-basis-point December rate hike and an 8% chance of a 50-basis-point increase, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Silver fell 5.3%, platinum declined 4.6%, and palladium lost 2.6%.

Nvidia stock extends losing streak amid congressional probe

Nvidia shares fell 2.5%, extending their decline to a fifth consecutive session as the House Committee on Energy and Commerce demanded a formal briefing over alleged export control violations.

Committee chairman Brett Guthrie requested that interim CEO Colette Kress arrange for company officials to appear before lawmakers by December 2.

The inquiry involves Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed and allegations that it helped Chinese companies circumvent US export restrictions.

Lawmakers are also examining claims that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department officials seeking information about the investigation.

Despite the scrutiny, analysts remain positive about Nvidia's business outlook.

The company reported third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion, up 103.2% year over year, and forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion.

Wedbush raised its price target to $293 from $275, while RBC and Morgan Stanley maintained positive ratings.

Nvidia's remaining $227.3 billion share buyback authorisation could also provide support for the stock.

data.title: SpaceX stock rises as Citi sees wireless network and AI growth potential
data.description:
SpaceX shares SPCX gained around 1.7% on Wednesday as investors assessed the company's expanding wireless ambitions, plans for artificial intelligence infrastructure in Texas and continued launch activity.

The stock also received support from positive analyst commentary.

Morgan Stanley reiterated its Overweight rating, suggesting investors consider buying shares during periods of weakness.

The brokerage said SpaceX had shown resilience despite volatility in AI-related stocks and could become a more durable holding as the market's AI investment theme evolves.

Meanwhile, Citi maintained its $280 price target on SpaceX, implying approximately 92% upside from current levels, as it examined the company's potential entry into the US mobile network market.

Citi sees SpaceX building its own mobile network

Citi believes SpaceX may need to develop a substantial ground-based network if it wants to compete with established US wireless operators, even as it plans to use Starlink satellites to reduce its reliance on traditional telecommunications infrastructure.

The brokerage highlighted comments from SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen at the TomorrowX Summit, where he outlined the company's plans for a wireless network that would rely less heavily on conventional cell towers.

SpaceX believes Starlink satellites could carry network traffic through space rather than depending as heavily on traditional fibre connections.

This could allow the company to operate a more efficient network using smaller cell sites.

However, Citi said a substantial number of macro cell sites would still be necessary, particularly in urban and suburban areas.

Ground infrastructure would help provide reliable indoor coverage and sufficient network capacity.

SpaceX could build its own network, acquire an existing telecommunications operator or operate as a mobile virtual network operator using another company's infrastructure.

Citi considers building its own network the most likely option.

Last month, SpaceX agreed to acquire Grain Management's nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz wireless spectrum licences, covering up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum.

The acquisition could strengthen Starlink Mobile's coverage, particularly indoors and in areas with weaker cellular signals.

JPMorgan had also highlighted the need for SpaceX to develop ground-based infrastructure to compete with established US telecom operators.

Texas approves SpaceX data centre and power project

SpaceX shares also gained after Texas resumed permitting for artificial intelligence facilities and approved the company's proposed data centre and natural-gas power plant, according to Politico.

The $24 billion project is located in the Rio Grande Valley, where SpaceX is headquartered.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued a permit allowing the company to install 35 natural-gas-powered turbines.

The facility is expected to generate 750 megawatts of electricity.

It will not be connected to the state's electrical grid, and the permit allows it to emit up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides annually.

The approval follows a September order by outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott to pause approvals for such projects.

Abbott lost his re-election bid earlier this month to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who won the election to become the state's next governor.

Upcoming Falcon 9 launch

SpaceX is also targeting Thursday, November 19, for a Falcon 9 launch of the USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

The four-hour launch window is scheduled to open at 6:46 p.m. Pacific time, or 9:46 p.m. Eastern. A backup opportunity is available on Friday, November 20, at 8:26 p.m. Pacific time.

The first-stage booster is scheduled to make its 11th flight, following previous launches including NROL-105, USSF-385 and eight Starlink missions.

SpaceX plans to land the booster on its Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.

data.title: Cathie Wood was right on the money about these 2 stocks
data.description:
Every new artificial intelligence (AI) data center needs chips.

The AI agents running on those chips need to fetch data, call software tools, and interact with websites.

Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management found winners on both sides of that buildout.

AMD and Cloudflare have seen explosive rallies since the famed investor first gained exposure to both.

They are proving a perfect example of how AI demand is spreading from the companies that supply the hardware to those that keep the applications running.

AMD turned a server-chip foothold into an AI business

ARK first bought about 640,000 AMD shares in the third quarter of 2018. At the time, they were going for about $31 only.

The firm later exited its position in Advanced Micro Devices, only to reestablish it in early 2023, at roughly $98 each.

As of writing, those same shares are trading at about $507 – suggesting Cathie Wood has secured a more than 5x gain on AMD.

The business behind that massive rally sells two kinds of chips into the same data center.

EPYC server processors handle general computing, while Instinct accelerators do the heavy lifting for AI models.

Demand for both pushed Q3 data center revenue up 97% to $8.5 billion.

The division’s operating profit climbed to $2.9 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier – showing how much of the sales growth is reaching the bottom line.

CEO Lisa Su expects data center chips to account for about 80% of AMD’s revenue in 2027.

That gives AMD more to gain as cloud companies expand capacity and more exposure if they slow the pace of new deployments.

Cloudflare found a way to turn developer adoption into revenue

Cloudflare first appeared in ARK’s reported holdings in the fourth quarter of 2020, when the stock traded at roughly $76.

In comparison, it’s now going for roughly $285, representing about 3.75x return on Cathie Wood’s initial investment.

The company now gives developers a place to run applications and AI agents through Workers – expanding what it can sell to businesses that already depend on its network for both security and performance.

Cloudflare passed 10 million active developers and added a record 158,000 paying customers in its fiscal Q3.

Revenue soared 39% to $782.5 million, and dollar-based net retention reached 122%.

That means the same group of customers generated 22% more revenue over a year after accounting for customers that cut spending or left.

Management also expects GAAP profitability in the fourth quarter, ahead of its earlier target of reaching that milestone by 2028.

The margin story helps explain why.

Workers carries a lower gross margin than some Cloudflare products, but it costs less to sell.

That gives Cloudflare a path to higher operating margins as developers turn experiments into applications they pay to run.

data.title: Can Anthropic IPO beat SpaceX to become the world's largest?
data.description:
Anthropic could price its shares above its proposed $70 to $78 range on Wednesday, putting the maker of Claude on course for one of the biggest stock market debuts ever.

Jay Ritter, director of the University of Florida’s IPO Initiative, told CNBC he expects the deal to “exceed SpaceX as the world’s largest IPO ever.”

At the $80 price he floated, however, Anthropic would still fall short on public proceeds under its current share count.

And for investors buying Anthropic stock as it goes live on Nasdaq, the bigger question is actually how much future profit that price already assumes.

What would it take to beat SpaceX?

At $80 a share, Anthropic’s planned sale of 825 million shares would generate $66 billion before fees, including proceeds going to existing shareholders.

That would rise to $75.9 billion if underwriters bought all the extra shares available to them.

SpaceX’s June debut brought in $75 billion initially and about $85.7 billion after its underwriters exercised their option.

On that like-for-like comparison, Anthropic would need a price above $90 per share with its extra allotment fully used, or a larger offering.

The separate $26 billion private placement with investors including Google and Nvidia boosts the total raised alongside the listing.

But the IPO record counts money raised only through the public offering itself.

Ritter sees a first-day jump in Anthropic stock

Ritter said the shares were “very likely to jump” from his hypothetical $80 offer price.

But using his estimates of a $1.5 trillion valuation and $35.2 billion in trailing 12-month revenue, investors would be paying roughly 43 times annual sales.

In plain terms, that’s about $43 in company value for every dollar Anthropic generated in revenue over the previous year, before paying for the computing power and other costs needed to serve customers.

Ritter said that multiple could look conservative next to Palantir or SpaceX, but “a lot of things have to go right.”

One is keeping customers willing to pay premium prices as competing AI models improve.

Investors who bought SpaceX shares at the time of the IPO haven't done well, with the stock falling 10% since its debut.

What investors are buying beyond the growth story

Ritter also pointed to Anthropic’s public benefit structure as a sign that it takes AI safety seriously.

Its directors must weigh shareholders’ financial interests alongside the interests of people affected by the company and its stated public mission.

In practice, the board has room to back a safety decision even if it slows a product launch or raises costs.

Anthropic’s prospectus says its public benefit initiatives could reduce profitability per share.

The final offer price will settle how close Anthropic gets to SpaceX’s record. For anyone buying after trading starts, a first-day jump raises the bar.

The higher the entry price, the more profit Anthropic must eventually deliver to justify it.

data.title: Strategy stock falls as analyst warns MSTR could crash to $23
data.description:
Strategy (formerly known as MicroStrategy) MSTR shares fell 4% on Wednesday as a prominent technical analyst warned that the Bitcoin-holding company's stock could plunge to $23, implying a potential decline of approximately 76% from its previous close.

Aksel Kibar, a widely followed Chartered Market Technician (CMT), based his warning on a bearish head-and-shoulders pattern on Strategy's daily share-price chart.

The stock closed at $96.50 on Tuesday, putting the analyst's price target well below its current trading level.

The warning comes as Strategy shares have already lost more than half their value over the past year.

The company has also faced pressure following MSCI's decision to exclude its shares from certain equity indices, raising concerns about its ability to raise capital for further Bitcoin purchases.

Head-and-shoulders pattern signals further downside

Kibar said the head-and-shoulders formation on Strategy's chart remained intact after the stock broke below its neckline earlier this year.

"The H&S top neckline was breached at 101 levels. Then we have seen a sharp rebound that did not negate the pattern with a breach above the high of the right shoulder. The pattern is intact, with a price target of 23," Kibar said in a post on X.

A head-and-shoulders pattern is a technical chart formation characterised by three peaks.

The middle peak, known as the head, is higher than the two surrounding peaks, or shoulders. The lows between these peaks form a support line called the neckline.

The pattern is generally considered bearish when it appears after a substantial price rally.

A break below the neckline can signal a potential reversal, with the price target calculated by measuring the distance between the head and the neckline and projecting it below the breakdown level.

In Strategy's case, the stock fell below the neckline around $101 during the third quarter before rebounding.

However, according to Kibar, the recovery did not rise above the high of the right shoulder, which would have invalidated the formation.

That leaves the bearish technical signal in place, although the $23 level represents an analyst's chart-based projection rather than a guaranteed outcome.

Bitcoin price remains important for Strategy stock

Kibar also linked Strategy's share-price outlook to Bitcoin, given the company's substantial exposure to the cryptocurrency.

On Bitcoin's price chart, the analyst identified a trading range between $60,000 and $82,800.

The range has a lower boundary, or floor, and an upper boundary, or ceiling.

A move below the $60,000 level could signal a continuation of the cryptocurrency's broader downtrend, according to Kibar.

Strategy's shares tend to track Bitcoin's price movements because of the company's large cryptocurrency holdings.

This makes the digital asset's direction an important factor for investors assessing the stock's prospects.

MSCI exclusion adds to investor concerns

Strategy's technical weakness comes alongside concerns about its access to capital.

MSCI recently announced that it would exclude Strategy from its equity indices.

The decision has raised questions about potential pressure on demand for the stock and the company's ability to raise fresh funds to finance additional Bitcoin purchases.

Strategy held 850,849 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $55 billion at the time of writing.

The company's large holdings make it one of the biggest corporate owners of Bitcoin and leave its stock closely tied to the cryptocurrency market.
